newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Moody's not planning Argentine upgrade--analyst.
newsitem.headline: Moody's not planning Argentine upgrade--analyst.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service Inc does not think Argentina's risk has fallen enough to raise the country's credit rating, Moody's lead Argentine analyst Kristin Lindow said in an interview published Tuesday.

"We have no fixed calendar for credit reviews. We do not feel pressured by what our competitors decide to do, nor by those that issue Argentine bonds, and we do not think Argentina's risk has fallen sufficiently to raise the rating," Lindow told the business daily El Cronista. "For now the outlook is stable."
Standard & Poor's Corp recently raised Argentina's long-term foreign currency debt rating to BB from BB-. Moody's rates Argentina B1.
Lindow said that in the last Moody's report on Argentina, it predicted that at the end of 1997 the country's total public and private debt would stand at $118 billion.
"That level has probably already been reached," she said, and the year-end total is likely to be $125 billion to $130 billion.

"I am worried that Argentina's government continues to distinguish between foreign and domestic debt in its foreign currency debt issues. That is complacent. If things go badly, the first people to sell off their papers will be the Argentines," Lindow said.

She said the main indicators to evaluate a developing country continue to be the ratios between debt, debt servicing costs and exports. Argentina's total debt is equivalent to 373 percent of exports, and its debt servicing costs amount to 56 percent of exports.
That compares with an average 149 percent and 24 percent, respectively, for all speculative-grade countries rated by Moody's.

"There has been very important and positive structural reforms, helped by a steep rise in debt. The economy is in a position to aspire to a better future, but with heavy indebtedness. This makes it more vulnerable to international shocks," said Lindow.
